claim: In oscillatory systems, neuronal activity phase is often independent of network frequency.
source: In oscillatory systems, neuronal activity phase is often independent of network frequency.
evidence: This is a general statement about oscillatory systems presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this sentence, but is supported by citations and data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Phase maintenance requires adjustment of synaptic input with network frequency.
source: Such phase maintenance requires adjustment of synaptic input with network frequency, a relationship that we explored using the crab, Cancer borealis, pyloric network.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript using the Cancer borealis pyloric network.

claim: The burst phase of pyloric neurons is relatively constant despite a > two fold variation in network frequency.
source: The burst phase of pyloric neurons is relatively constant despite a > two fold variation in network frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 1 and related experiments.

claim: Phase constancy across a range of periods required a proportional increase of synaptic duration with period.
source: Phase constancy across a range of periods required a proportional increase of synaptic duration with period.
evidence: This finding is supported by dynamic clamp experiments comparing constant duration vs. constant duty cycle conditions.

claim: Phase maintenance was promoted by an increase of amplitude and peak phase of synaptic input with period.
source: However, phase maintenance was also promoted by an increase of amplitude and peak phase of synaptic input with period.
evidence: This is demonstrated through systematic dynamic clamp experiments varying gmax and Δpeak as shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Short-term synaptic plasticity can coordinately change amplitude and peak phase to maximize the range of periods over which phase constancy is achieved.
source: Mathematical analysis shows how short-term synaptic plasticity can coordinately change amplitude and peak phase to maximize the range of periods over which phase constancy is achieved.
evidence: This is supported by mathematical modeling presented in the Materials and methods section and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Oscillatory neural activity is often organized into different phases across groups of neurons in brain rhythms associated with cognitive tasks or behavioral states.
source: Oscillatory neural activity is often organized into different phases across groups of neurons, both in brain rhythms associated with cognitive tasks or behavioral states (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018), and in central pattern generating (CPG) circuits that drive rhythmic motor behaviors (Marder and Bucher, 2001; Marder et al., 2005; Grillner, 2006; Bucher et al., 2015; Katz, 2016; Stein, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Oscillatory neural activity is often organized into different phases across groups of neurons in central pattern generating (CPG) circuits that drive rhythmic motor behaviors.
source: Oscillatory neural activity is often organized into different phases across groups of neurons, both in brain rhythms associated with cognitive tasks or behavioral states (Hasselmo et al., 2002; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018), and in central pattern generating (CPG) circuits that drive rhythmic motor behaviors (Marder and Bucher, 2001; Marder et al., 2005; Grillner, 2006; Bucher et al., 2015; Katz, 2016; Stein, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Different phases in motor circuits provide alternating flexion and extension of limb joints, and coordination of movements between joints, limbs, and segments.
source: The functional significance of different phases in the latter is readily apparent, as they for example provide alternating flexion and extension of limb joints, and coordination of movements between joints, limbs, and segments (Krantz and Parks, 2012; Grillner and El Manira, 2015; Kiehn, 2016; Le Gal et al., 2017; Bidaye et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on motor control.

claim: A hallmark of many motor patterns is that the relative timing of firing between neurons is well maintained over a range of rhythm frequencies.
source: A hallmark of many such patterns is that the relative timing of firing between neurons is well maintained over a range of rhythm frequencies (Dicaprio et al., 1997; Hooper, 1997b; Hooper, 1997a; Wenning et al., 2004; Marder et al., 2005; Grillner, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011; Le Gal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: If the latency of firing across different groups of neurons changes proportionally to the rhythm period, phase (latency over period) is invariant.
source: If the latency of firing across different groups of neurons changes proportionally to the rhythm period, phase (latency over period) is invariant, in some cases providing optimal limb coordination at all speeds (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a mathematical definition supported by citation.

claim: Phase invariance can provide optimal limb coordination at all speeds.
source: If the latency of firing across different groups of neurons changes proportionally to the rhythm period, phase (latency over period) is invariant, in some cases providing optimal limb coordination at all speeds (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The ability of the system to coordinate phases with changes in period arises from central coordinating mechanisms between circuit elements.
source: The ability of the system to coordinate phases with changes in period arises from central coordinating mechanisms between circuit elements, as it is present in isolated nervous system preparations, but the underlying cellular and circuit mechanisms are not well understood.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phase coordination is present in isolated nervous system preparations.

claim: Constant phase lags between neighboring segments in the control of swimming in lamprey fish and crayfish can be explained mathematically on the basis of asymmetrically weakly coupled oscillators.
source: For instance, constant phase lags between neighboring segments in the control of swimming in lamprey fish and crayfish can be explained mathematically on the basis of asymmetrically weakly coupled oscillators, but the role of intrinsic and synaptic dynamics within each segment is unknown (Cohen et al., 1992; Skinner and Mulloney, 1998; Grillner, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2014; Le Gal et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior mathematical modeling work.

claim: The role of intrinsic and synaptic dynamics within each segment in lamprey and crayfish swimming is unknown.
source: For instance, constant phase lags between neighboring segments in the control of swimming in lamprey fish and crayfish can be explained mathematically on the basis of asymmetrically weakly coupled oscillators, but the role of intrinsic and synaptic dynamics within each segment is unknown (Cohen et al., 1992; Skinner and Mulloney, 1998; Grillner, 2006; Mullins et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2014; Le Gal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge despite mathematical explanations.

claim: The pyloric circuit generates a triphasic motor pattern with stable phase relationships over a wide range of periods.
source: The pyloric circuit generates a triphasic motor pattern with stable phase relationships over a wide range of periods (Eisen and Marder, 1984; Hooper, 1997b; Hooper, 1997a; Bucher et al., 2005; Goaillard et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2012; Soofi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Synapses in the pyloric circuit use graded as well as spike-mediated transmission.
source: Synapses in the pyloric circuit use graded as well as spike-mediated transmission (Graubard et al., 1980; Harris-Warrick and Johnson, 2010; Zhao et al., 2011; Rosenbaum and Marder, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Follower neurons burst in rebound from inhibition from pacemaker neurons.
source: Follower neurons burst in rebound from inhibition from pacemaker neurons (Marder and Bucher, 2007; Daur et al., 2016), and post-inhibitory rebound delay scales with the period of hyperpolarizing currents (Hooper, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Post-inhibitory rebound delay scales with the period of hyperpolarizing currents.
source: Follower neurons burst in rebound from inhibition from pacemaker neurons (Marder and Bucher, 2007; Daur et al., 2016), and post-inhibitory rebound delay scales with the period of hyperpolarizing currents (Hooper, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Voltage-gated conductances slow enough for cumulative activation across cycles could promote phase maintenance.
source: Voltage-gated conductances slow enough for cumulative activation across cycles could promote such phase maintenance (Hooper et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Short-term depression of graded inhibitory synapses is slow enough to accumulate over several pyloric cycles.
source: Similarly, short-term depression of graded inhibitory synapses is slow enough to accumulate over several pyloric cycles, meaning that effective synaptic strength increases with increasing cycle period (Manor et al., 1997; Nadim and Manor, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Effective synaptic strength increases with increasing cycle period due to short-term depression.
source: Similarly, short-term depression of graded inhibitory synapses is slow enough to accumulate over several pyloric cycles, meaning that effective synaptic strength increases with increasing cycle period (Manor et al., 1997; Nadim and Manor, 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the accumulation of short-term depression and supported by citations.

claim: Short-term synaptic depression, by increasing inhibition strength with cycle period, should promote phase maintenance.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that short-term synaptic depression, by increasing inhibition strength with cycle period, should promote phase maintenance (Manor et al., 2003; Mouser et al., 2008), particularly in conjunction with inactivating (A-type) potassium currents (Bose et al., 2004; Greenberg and Manor, 2005), which control the rebound delay (Harris-Warrick et al., 1995b; Harris-Warrick et al., 1995a; Kloppenburg et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical/modeling studies.

claim: Short-term synaptic depression promotes phase maintenance particularly in conjunction with inactivating (A-type) potassium currents.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that short-term synaptic depression, by increasing inhibition strength with cycle period, should promote phase maintenance (Manor et al., 2003; Mouser et al., 2008), particularly in conjunction with inactivating (A-type) potassium currents (Bose et al., 2004; Greenberg and Manor, 2005), which control the rebound delay (Harris-Warrick et al., 1995b; Harris-Warrick et al., 1995a; Kloppenburg et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical/modeling studies.

claim: A-type potassium currents control the rebound delay.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that short-term synaptic depression, by increasing inhibition strength with cycle period, should promote phase maintenance (Manor et al., 2003; Mouser et al., 2008), particularly in conjunction with inactivating (A-type) potassium currents (Bose et al., 2004; Greenberg and Manor, 2005), which control the rebound delay (Harris-Warrick et al., 1995b; Harris-Warrick et al., 1995a; Kloppenburg et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The predictions about short-term synaptic depression promoting phase maintenance remain experimentally untested.
source: These predictions remain experimentally untested.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Postsynaptic responses depend on the actual trajectory of synaptic conductances, which are shaped by presynaptic voltage trajectories and short-term synaptic plasticity.
source: Additionally, postsynaptic responses also depend on the actual trajectory of synaptic conductances, which are shaped by presynaptic voltage trajectories and short-term synaptic plasticity (Manor et al., 1997; Mamiya et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2011; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: If amplitude, duration, and trajectory of synaptic conductance determine rebound delay, phase maintenance necessitates all three of these parameters to change with cycle period in coordination.
source: If amplitude, duration, and trajectory of synaptic conductance determine rebound delay, phase maintenance necessitates all three of these parameters to change with cycle period in coordination.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between synaptic parameters and rebound delay.

claim: The overall burst onset phase of the LP neuron was measured to be φLP=0.34 ± 0.03 (N = 9).
source: We measured an overall burst onset phase of the LP neuron to be φLP=0.34 ± 0.03 (N = 9).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: IBI had a significant effect on peak amplitude Iamp (p<0.001).
source: IBI had a significant effect on amplitude Iamp (p<0.001), peak phase Δpeak (p<0.001), slopeup (p<0.001) and slopedown (p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of burst-triggered averaging data.

claim: IBI had a significant effect on peak phase Δpeak (p<0.001).
source: IBI had a significant effect on amplitude Iamp (p<0.001), peak phase Δpeak (p<0.001), slopeup (p<0.001) and slopedown (p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of burst-triggered averaging data.

claim: IBI had a significant effect on slopeup (p<0.001).
source: IBI had a significant effect on amplitude Iamp (p<0.001), peak phase Δpeak (p<0.001), slopeup (p<0.001) and slopedown (p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of burst-triggered averaging data.

claim: IBI had a significant effect on slopedown (p=0.002).
source: IBI had a significant effect on amplitude Iamp (p<0.001), peak phase Δpeak (p<0.001), slopeup (p<0.001) and slopedown (p=0.002).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of burst-triggered averaging data.

claim: Larger IBIs corresponded to larger Ipeak values (p<0.001, χ2 = 65.87).
source: In particular, larger IBIs corresponded to larger Ipeak values (Figure 2F–2H; p<0.001, χ2 = 65.87) with smaller (more advanced) Δpeak (Figure 2I; p<0.001, χ2 = 41.35).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2F-2H.

claim: Larger IBIs corresponded to smaller (more advanced) Δpeak (p<0.001, χ2 = 41.35).
source: In particular, larger IBIs corresponded to larger Ipeak values (Figure 2F–2H; p<0.001, χ2 = 65.87) with smaller (more advanced) Δpeak (Figure 2I; p<0.001, χ2 = 41.35).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The change in Δpeak was due to a decrease in slopeup (p<0.001, χ2 = 65.25).
source: The change in Δpeak was due to a decrease in slopeup (p<0.001, χ2 = 65.25), whereas slopedown did not vary as much (Figure 2J–2K; p=0.002, χ2 = 14.77).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2J-2K.

claim: Slopedown did not vary as much with IBI (p=0.002, χ2 = 14.77).
source: The change in Δpeak was due to a decrease in slopeup (p<0.001, χ2 = 65.25), whereas slopedown did not vary as much (Figure 2J–2K; p=0.002, χ2 = 14.77).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2J-2K.

claim: The synaptic current to the LP neuron always had a single peak in each cycle.
source: In each cycle, the synaptic current always had a single peak, but the amplitude and phase of this peak showed variability across preparations (Figure 3B, average in blue).
evidence: This is an observation from voltage clamp measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The amplitude and phase of the synaptic current peak showed variability across preparations.
source: In each cycle, the synaptic current always had a single peak, but the amplitude and phase of this peak showed variability across preparations (Figure 3B, average in blue).
evidence: This is an observation from voltage clamp measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For any fixed gmax, φLP decreased as a function of P.
source: For any fixed gmax, φLP decreased as a function of P (Figure 3D), that is the relative onset of the LP burst was advanced in slower rhythms.
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The relative onset of the LP burst was advanced in slower rhythms.
source: For any fixed gmax, φLP decreased as a function of P (Figure 3D), that is the relative onset of the LP burst was advanced in slower rhythms.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the decrease in φLP with increasing P.

claim: For any given P, φLP increased sublinearly as a function of gmax.
source: In contrast to the effect of P, for any given P, φLP increased sublinearly as a function of gmax (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The LP neuron intrinsic properties alone do not produce phase constancy.
source: The results shown in Figure 3D indicate that the LP neuron intrinsic properties alone do not produce phase constancy.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that φLP decreases with P when gmax is held constant.

claim: Phase could be maintained over a range of P values if gmax increases as a function of P.
source: However, level sets of φLP (highlighted for three values in Figure 3F), indicate that phase could be maintained over a range of P values, if gmax increases as a function of P.
evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of level sets in Figure 3F.

claim: The LP neuron produced burst responses that followed the synaptic input in a 1:1 manner across all values of P that were used.
source: The LP neuron produced burst responses that followed the synaptic input in a 1:1 manner across all values of P that were used (Figure 6A1).
evidence: This is an observation from dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 6A1.

claim: When gmax and Δpeak were kept constant, φLP decreased as a function of P.
source: When gmax and Δpeak were kept constant, φLP decreased as a function of P (Figure 6A2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 6A2.

claim: The decrease in φLP with P was always larger for the C-Dur case than the C-DC case.
source: This decrease was always larger for the C-Dur case than the C-DC case.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the two conditions in the experiments.

claim: The effect of P on φLP was highly significant for both C-DC (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 100.677) and C-Dur (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 466.424).
source: The effect of P on φLP was highly significant for both C-DC (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 100.677) and C-Dur (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 466.424), indicating that the period and duration of the inhibitory input to the LP neuron had a significant effect on its phase.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The period and duration of the inhibitory input to the LP neuron had a significant effect on its phase.
source: The effect of P on φLP was highly significant for both C-DC (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 100.677) and C-Dur (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 466.424), indicating that the period and duration of the inhibitory input to the LP neuron had a significant effect on its phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the statistical significance of P effects.

claim: Increasing gmax at constant values of P and Δpeak produced a significant but only small to moderate increase in φLP (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 10.798).
source: Overall, increasing gmax at constant values of P and Δpeak produced a significant but only small to moderate increase in φLP (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 10.798).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: φLP in the C-DC case was restricted to a smaller range compared to C-Dur.
source: Although increasing gmax produced the same qualitative effect for both the C-DC and C-Dur (e.g., Figure 6B2), φLP in the C-DC case was restricted to a smaller range (Figure 6B3 top vs. bottom panels).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the ranges in Figure 6B3.

claim: Increasing Δpeak for a constant value of P and gmax produced a small but significant increase in φLP (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 17.172).
source: Increasing Δpeak for a constant value of P and gmax (Figure 6C1), produced a small but significant increase in φLP (three-way ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 17.172).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: All three parameters that define the shape of the IPSC (P, gmax, and Δpeak) influence φLP.
source: These results showed that all three parameters that define the shape of the IPSC influence φLP.
evidence: This is concluded from the systematic exploration of these parameters.

claim: The strongest effect on φLP is the decrease in φLP as a function of P.
source: Clearly, the strongest effect is the decrease in φLP as a function of P.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the magnitudes of effects of different parameters.

claim: φLP modestly increases as a function of gmax and Δpeak.
source: However, φLP modestly increases as a function of the other two parameters, gmax and Δpeak.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results.

claim: Sensitivity of φLP to gmax and Δpeak varied across P values, with larger sensitivity at lower values of P (two-way RM-ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 16.054).
source: Sensitivity of φLP to these two parameters varied across P values, with larger sensitivity at lower values of P (two-way RM-ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 16.054; data included in Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of sensitivity measurements.

claim: For the C-DC case, φLP had a positive sensitivity to gmax and a smaller positive sensitivity to Δpeak.
source: These results showed that, for the C-DC case, φLP had a positive sensitivity to gmax and a smaller positive sensitivity to Δpeak (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown by sensitivity analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: The sensitivity was largest if gmax and Δpeak were varied together and smallest if they were varied in opposite directions for the C-DC case (two-way RM-ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 3.330).
source: The sensitivity was largest if the two parameters were varied together (gmax + Δpeak) and smallest if they were varied in opposite directions (gmax - Δpeak; two-way RM-ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 3.330).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of sensitivity measurements for the C-DC case.

claim: Sensitivity values were significantly different for the C-Dur case (two-way RM-ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 2.892), with largest sensitivity for gmax + Δpeak and smallest for gmax - Δpeak.
source: Similarly, these sensitivity values were also significantly different for the C-Dur case (Figure 7B; two-way RM-ANOVA, p<0.001, F = 2.892), with largest sensitivity for gmax + Δpeak and smallest for gmax - Δpeak.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of sensitivity measurements for the C-Dur case shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The LP neuron could not achieve phases below 0.3 in the C-DC case.
source: We found that the LP neuron could not achieve phases below 0.3 in the C-DC case (Figure 8C1), which is simply because the neuron never fired during the inhibitory synaptic current (which had a duty cycle of 0.3).
evidence: This is observed from the data in Figure 8C1 and explained by the duty cycle constraint.

claim: The neuron never fired during the inhibitory synaptic current in the C-DC case.
source: We found that the LP neuron could not achieve phases below 0.3 in the C-DC case (Figure 8C1), which is simply because the neuron never fired during the inhibitory synaptic current (which had a duty cycle of 0.3).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The range of P values for which the LP phase could be maintained by varying gmax and Δpeak was much larger for C-DC inputs compared to C-Dur inputs, for all φc values between 0.31 and 0.54.
source: Furthermore, the range of P values for which the LP phase could be maintained by varying gmax and Δpeak was much larger for C-DC inputs compared to C-Dur Inputs, for all φc values between 0.31 and 0.54.
evidence: This is concluded from analysis of the level sets shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the C-Dur case, as P increased, φLP decayed and approached 0 like 1/P.
source: In the C-Dur case (Equation (7)), as P increased, φLP decayed and approached 0 like 1/P.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model (Equation 7).

claim: In the C-DC case, φLP approached its lower limit Δpeak·DC as P increased.
source: In contrast, in the C-DC case (Equation (8)), φLP approached its lower limit Δpeak·DC, as P increased, and thus behaved very differently than in the C-Dur case.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model (Equation 8).

claim: Phase constancy can be achieved by varying either gmax or Δpeak, but each parameter produces a different range of P across which phase is maintained.
source: As the figure shows, phase constancy can be achieved by varying either parameter, but each parameter produces a different range of P across which phase is maintained.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical model shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The pacemaker synaptic input to the LP neuron shows short-term synaptic depression.
source: The pacemaker synaptic input to the LP neuron shows short-term synaptic depression (Rabbah and Nadim, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: When synaptic depression dictates how gmax varies with P and Δpeak also varies with P and gmax, the simultaneous changes in gmax and Δpeak greatly increase the range of P values over which φLP is constant.
source: When synaptic depression dictates how gmax varies with P and Δpeak also varies with P and gmax (Equation (11)), the simultaneous changes in gmax and Δpeak (red) greatly increase the range of P values over which φLP is constant (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical model shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The C-DC case with short-term depression spans a larger range of P values than the non-depressing case.
source: Note that the C-DC case with short-term depression spans a larger range of P values than the non-depressing case (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical model shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The range of P values for which phase can be maintained is larger with depression than the non-depressing case across φLP values, except where φLP is so large that the depressing synapse operates outside its dynamic range.
source: Similarly, the range of P values for which phase can be maintained is larger than the non-depressing case across φLP values, except where φLP is so large that the depressing synapse operates outside its dynamic range (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical model shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Although phase constancy can be achieved when either gmax or Δpeak increases with P, a concomitant increase of both greatly expands the range of P values for which a constant phase is maintained.
source: These results are consistent with our experimental results, indicating that although phase constancy can be achieved when either gmax or Δpeak increases with P, a concomitant increase of both - which could occur for example with a depressing synapse - greatly expands the range of P values for which a constant phase is maintained.
evidence: This is concluded from the mathematical model and experimental results.

claim: Different hippocampal and cortical neurons are active in at least three distinct phases of the gamma rhythm.
source: For example, different hippocampal and cortical neurons are active in at least three distinct phases of the gamma rhythm (Hájos et al., 2004; Hasenstaub et al., 2005), and distinct hippocampal neuron types fire at different phases of the theta rhythm and sharp wave-associated ripple episodes (Somogyi and Klausberger, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Distinct hippocampal neuron types fire at different phases of the theta rhythm and sharp wave-associated ripple episodes.
source: For example, different hippocampal and cortical neurons are active in at least three distinct phases of the gamma rhythm (Hájos et al., 2004; Hasenstaub et al., 2005), and distinct hippocampal neuron types fire at different phases of the theta rhythm and sharp wave-associated ripple episodes (Somogyi and Klausberger, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Distinct neuron types can maintain a coherent activity phase despite wide variations in the network frequency.
source: Distinct neuron types can maintain a coherent activity phase, despite wide variations in the network frequency (30–100 Hz for gamma rhythms, 4–7 Hz for theta rhythms, and 120–200 Hz for sharp wave-associated ripple episodes).
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about oscillatory networks.

claim: Phase-specific activity of different neuron types is proposed to be important in rhythm generation.
source: Phase-specific activity of different neuron types is proposed to be important in rhythm generation (Wang, 2010), and indicates the necessity of precise timing for producing proper circuit output and behavior (Kopell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Phase-specific activity indicates the necessity of precise timing for producing proper circuit output and behavior.
source: Phase-specific activity of different neuron types is proposed to be important in rhythm generation (Wang, 2010), and indicates the necessity of precise timing for producing proper circuit output and behavior (Kopell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Phase locking of spike patterns to oscillations is important for auditory processing, single cell and network computations and Hebbian learning rules.
source: For example, phase locking of spike patterns to oscillations is important for auditory processing, single cell and network computations and Hebbian learning rules (Kayser et al., 2009; McLelland and Paulsen, 2009; Panzeri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The activity phase of distinct neuron types in rhythmic motor circuits is a tangible readout of the timing of motor neurons and muscle contractions, thus defining phases of movement.
source: In contrast, the activity phase of distinct neuron types in rhythmic motor circuits is a tangible readout of the timing of motor neurons and muscle contractions, thus defining phases of movement (Grillner and El Manira, 2015; Kiehn, 2016; Le Gal et al., 2017; Bidaye et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on motor control.

claim: Whether neurons maintain their activity phase in face of changes in frequency translates to whether the movement pattern changes as it speeds up or slows down.
source: Because meaningful behavior depends crucially on proper activity phases, whether neurons maintain their activity phase in face of changes in frequency simply translates to whether the movement pattern changes as it speeds up or slows down.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between phase maintenance and motor behavior.

claim: The timing of the LP neuron is strongly dependent on the timing of inputs it receives.
source: Our results from noise current injections showed that the timing of the LP neuron is strongly dependent on the timing of inputs it receives.
evidence: This is concluded from the noise injection experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: φLP was largely determined by the duration of the synaptic input.
source: Dynamic clamp injection of realistic or triangular conductance waveforms with different periods (P) indicated that φLP was largely determined by the duration of the synaptic input.
evidence: This is concluded from the dynamic clamp experiments comparing C-Dur and C-DC conditions.

claim: φLP changed substantially with P when inputs had constant duration.
source: φLP changed substantially with P when inputs had constant duration, but much less when inputs had a constant duty cycle, that is when duration scaled with P.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: φLP changed much less with P when inputs had a constant duty cycle.
source: φLP changed substantially with P when inputs had constant duration, but much less when inputs had a constant duty cycle, that is when duration scaled with P.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inputs of constant duty cycles alone are insufficient for phase constancy.
source: However, our experiments also showed that inputs of constant duty cycles alone are insufficient for phase constancy.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that φLP still decreased with P even with constant duty cycle.

claim: φLP decreased with P even with a constant duty cycle of inputs.
source: φLP decreased with P even with a constant duty cycle of inputs, but increased with either synaptic strength (gmax) or peak phase of the synaptic input (Δpeak).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dynamic clamp experiments.

claim: φLP increased with either synaptic strength (gmax) or peak phase of the synaptic input (Δpeak).
source: φLP decreased with P even with a constant duty cycle of inputs, but increased with either synaptic strength (gmax) or peak phase of the synaptic input (Δpeak).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dynamic clamp experiments shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The increase in φLP had similar sensitivity to gmax and Δpeak.
source: The increase in φLP had similar sensitivity to gmax and Δpeak, and therefore a larger sensitivity to a simultaneous increase in both.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: φLP had a larger sensitivity to a simultaneous increase in both gmax and Δpeak.
source: The increase in φLP had similar sensitivity to gmax and Δpeak, and therefore a larger sensitivity to a simultaneous increase in both.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: It was possible to keep φLP constant over a wide range of cycle periods by increasing both gmax and Δpeak with P.
source: Consequently, it was possible to keep φLP constant over a wide range of cycle periods by increasing both parameters with P.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental results and level set analysis.

claim: The fact that an increase in gmax with P promotes phase constancy is biologically relevant, as short-term depression in pyloric synapses means that synaptic strength indeed increases with P.
source: The fact that an increase in gmax with P promotes phase constancy is biologically relevant, as short-term depression in pyloric synapses means that synaptic strength indeed increases with P (Manor et al., 1997).
evidence: This connects the experimental findings to known biological properties, supported by citation.

claim: Δpeak in LP actually decreases with P.
source: The finding that an increase of Δpeak with P promotes phase maintenance is somewhat surprising, as we have previously shown that Δpeak in LP actually decreases with P (Manor et al., 1997; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: When P is changed in an individual preparation by injecting current into or voltage-clamping the pacemakers, phase of follower neurons is not particularly well maintained.
source: When P is changed in an individual preparation by injecting current into or voltage-clamping the pacemakers, phase of follower neurons is not particularly well maintained.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experiments, with Figure 1 as an example.

claim: All pyloric neurons show behavior that falls between constant phase and constant latencies when P is changed by manipulating pacemakers.
source: An example of this is shown in Figure 1, where φLP values fall between constant phase and constant duration and, additionally, all pyloric neurons show behavior that falls between constant phase and constant latencies (Hooper, 1997b; Hooper, 1997a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: Neurons are not keeping phase particularly well when the only cause of changing P is the presynaptic input.
source: This may reflect that neurons are not keeping phase particularly well when the only cause of changing P is the presynaptic input.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phase is not well maintained when P is changed by manipulating pacemakers.

claim: Even during normal ongoing pyloric activity, phases change with cycle-to-cycle variability of P in individual preparations.
source: This is supported by the observation that even during normal ongoing pyloric activity, phases change with cycle-to-cycle variability of P in individual preparations (Bucher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Δpeak may play an important role in stable phase relationships when P differs because of temperature, neuromodulatory conditions, or inter-individual variability.
source: However, it does not preclude the possibility that Δpeak plays an important role in stable phase relationships when P differs because of temperature, neuromodulatory conditions, or inter-individual variability (discussed below).
evidence: This is speculation about potential roles of Δpeak under different conditions.

claim: Short-term synaptic plasticity can act as a frequency-dependent gain control mechanism for many spike-mediated synaptic connections.
source: It is noteworthy that a change in the synaptic strength or peak phase with P is not peculiar to graded synapses. The fact that short-term synaptic plasticity can act as a frequency-dependent gain control mechanism is well known for many spike-mediated synaptic connections.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about synaptic plasticity.

claim: In bursting neurons, the presence of a combination of short-term depression and facilitation in the same spike-mediated synaptic interaction could result in changes in the peak phase of the summated synaptic current as a function of burst frequency and duration, and the intra-burst spike rate.
source: In bursting neurons, the presence of a combination of short-term depression and facilitation in the same spike-mediated synaptic interaction could also result in changes in the peak phase of the summated synaptic current as a function of burst frequency and duration, and the intra-burst spike rate (Markram et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The mathematical model provides mechanistic explanations for several experimental findings.
source: The mathematical model in the current study provides mechanistic explanations for several of our experimental findings.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the model's utility.

claim: The mathematical model can be used to produce a quantitative measure of phase, given the values of gmax, Δpeak and P.
source: First, it can be used to produce a quantitative measure of phase, given the values of gmax, Δpeak and P.
evidence: This describes the capability of the mathematical model.

claim: The mathematical equations can be used to compare the C-DC and C-Dur cases, which match experimental results.
source: Thus, these equations can be used to compare the C-DC and C-Dur cases, which match our experimental results.
evidence: This describes how the model predictions match experimental observations.

claim: The mathematical equations provide the activity phase no matter how the pacemaker synaptic input duration changes with cycle period.
source: Second, these equations provide the activity phase no matter how the pacemaker synaptic input duration changes with cycle period.
evidence: This describes the generality of the mathematical model.

claim: The combined increase in gmax and Δpeak with P produces a larger range of periods for phase constancy than increasing either parameter alone.
source: Moreover, we showed that the combined increase in gmax and Δpeak with P produces a larger range of periods for phase constancy than increasing either parameter alone.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mathematical model shown in Figure 9.

claim: The timing of post-inhibitory spiking in LP neurons was relatively stable across preparations.
source: These data were not included in this study for brevity and because they showed that the timing of post-inhibitory spiking was relatively stable across preparations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from separate experiments not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The contribution of intrinsic properties in controlling the timing of the LP neuron burst onset is expected to be relatively small.
source: Therefore, we would expect the contribution of intrinsic properties in controlling the timing of the LP neuron burst onset to be relatively small.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that post-inhibitory spiking timing was stable across preparations.

claim: The follower ventral dilator (VD) and PY neurons have a much higher levels of IA than LP.
source: For example, the follower ventral dilator (VD) and PY neurons have a much higher levels of IA, which in turn has a larger effect on the timing of post-inhibitory spiking.
evidence: This is stated as known information about these neurons.

claim: IA has a larger effect on the timing of post-inhibitory spiking in VD and PY neurons.
source: For example, the follower ventral dilator (VD) and PY neurons have a much higher levels of IA, which in turn has a larger effect on the timing of post-inhibitory spiking.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher levels of IA in these neurons.

claim: Tang et al. (2012) report a fourfold decrease in P of the pyloric rhythm between 7 and 23° C.
source: Tang et al. (2012) report a fourfold decrease in P of the pyloric rhythm between 7 and 23° C.
evidence: This is a citation to prior experimental work.

claim: None of the pyloric phases changed significantly when temperature was changed between 7 and 23° C.
source: In this study, none of the pyloric phases changed significantly, and it is worth noting that under conditions of changing temperatures, the relationships between P, gmax, and Δpeak appeared to be fundamentally different from when P is changed at a constant temperature.
evidence: This is cited from Tang et al. (2012).

claim: Under conditions of changing temperatures, the relationships between P, gmax, and Δpeak appeared to be fundamentally different from when P is changed at a constant temperature.
source: In this study, none of the pyloric phases changed significantly, and it is worth noting that under conditions of changing temperatures, the relationships between P, gmax, and Δpeak appeared to be fundamentally different from when P is changed at a constant temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from observations in Tang et al. (2012).

claim: Presynaptic voltage trajectories scaled with changing P when temperature was changed.
source: Presynaptic voltage trajectories scaled with changing P, and Δpeak of postsynaptic currents was independent of P, in contrast to the decrease described at constant temperature (Manor et al., 1997; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Tang et al. (2012) and contrasted with other studies.

claim: Δpeak of postsynaptic currents was independent of P when temperature was changed.
source: Presynaptic voltage trajectories scaled with changing P, and Δpeak of postsynaptic currents was independent of P, in contrast to the decrease described at constant temperature (Manor et al., 1997; Tseng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from Tang et al. (2012) and contrasted with other studies.

claim: Amplitudes of synaptic potentials did not change with temperature, despite an increase in synaptic current amplitudes with increasing temperature.
source: Amplitudes of synaptic potentials did not change with temperature, despite an increase in synaptic current amplitudes with increasing temperature (and associated decrease in P).
evidence: This is cited from Tang et al. (2012).

claim: The effects of temperature on synaptic dynamics and ion channel gating are subject to a set of compensatory adaptations different from when P is changed at constant temperature.
source: Therefore, it appears that the likely substantial effects of temperature on synaptic dynamics and ion channel gating are subject to a set of compensatory adaptations different from when P is changed at constant temperature.
evidence: This is inferred from the different relationships between parameters when temperature is changed.

claim: Phase maintenance in the face of changing P in an individual animal requires the appropriate short-term dynamics of synaptic and intrinsic neuronal properties.
source: Phase maintenance in the face of changing P in an individual animal requires the appropriate short-term dynamics of synaptic and intrinsic neuronal properties.
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the study.

claim: Characteristic phase relationships can be observed under the same experimental conditions across individual preparations even when P varies substantially.
source: The fact that characteristic (and therefore similar) phase relationships can also be observed under the same experimental conditions across individual preparations is a different conundrum, particularly when P can vary substantially, as is true for brain oscillations (Hájos et al., 2004; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Somogyi and Klausberger, 2005).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to prior work.

claim: Phases show different degrees of variability across individuals in leech heartbeat, larval crawling in Drosophila, and fictive swimming in zebrafish.
source: Phases show different degrees of variability across individuals in a variety of systems, for example leech heartbeat (Wenning et al., 2018), larval crawling in Drosophila (Pulver et al., 2015), and fictive swimming in zebrafish (Masino and Fetcho, 2005), but in all these cases phases are not correlated with P.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In leech heartbeat, larval crawling in Drosophila, and fictive swimming in zebrafish, phases are not correlated with P.
source: Phases show different degrees of variability across individuals in a variety of systems, for example leech heartbeat (Wenning et al., 2018), larval crawling in Drosophila (Pulver et al., 2015), and fictive swimming in zebrafish (Masino and Fetcho, 2005), but in all these cases phases are not correlated with P.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the pyloric rhythm, phases are variable to a degree across individuals, but not correlated with the mean P, which varies >2 fold.
source: In the pyloric rhythm, phases are also variable to a degree across individuals, but not correlated with the mean P, which varies >2 fold (Bucher et al., 2005; Goaillard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phase constancy in the pyloric rhythm occurs despite considerable inter-individual variability in ionic currents.
source: This phase constancy occurs despite considerable inter-individual variability in ionic currents, and is considered the ultimate target of slow compensatory regulation, that is homeostatic plasticity (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Ma and LaMotte, 2007; Marder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Phase constancy is considered the ultimate target of slow compensatory regulation (homeostatic plasticity).
source: This phase constancy occurs despite considerable inter-individual variability in ionic currents, and is considered the ultimate target of slow compensatory regulation, that is homeostatic plasticity (Marder and Goaillard, 2006; Ma and LaMotte, 2007; Marder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Slow compensation can be observed directly when rhythmic activity is disrupted by decentralization, and subsequently recovers to similar phase relationships over the course of many hours.
source: Slow compensation can also be observed directly when rhythmic activity is disrupted by decentralization, and subsequently recovers to similar phase relationships over the course of many hours (Luther et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Synaptic inputs to the LP neuron show considerable variability across preparations.
source: Synaptic inputs to the LP neuron show considerable variability across preparations (e.g. Figure 3B), which mirrors the variability seen in the levels of voltage-gated ionic currents in pyloric neurons (Schulz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3B and supported by citation.

claim: The variability in synaptic inputs mirrors the variability seen in the levels of voltage-gated ionic currents in pyloric neurons.
source: Synaptic inputs to the LP neuron show considerable variability across preparations (e.g. Figure 3B), which mirrors the variability seen in the levels of voltage-gated ionic currents in pyloric neurons (Schulz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Changes in phase relationships are functionally important to produce qualitatively different versions of circuit output, for example to produce different gaits in locomotion.
source: In motor systems, in particular, changes in phase relationships are functionally important to produce qualitatively different versions of circuit output, for example to produce different gaits in locomotion (Vidal-Gadea et al., 2011; Grillner and El Manira, 2015; Kiehn, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on motor control.

claim: Much of the flexibility in neural circuit activity is provided by modulatory transmitters and hormones which alter synaptic and intrinsic neuronal properties.
source: The activity of neural circuits is flexible, and much of this flexibility is provided by modulatory transmitters and hormones which alter synaptic and intrinsic neuronal properties (Brezina, 2010; Harris-Warrick, 2011; Jordan and Sławińska, 2011; Bargmann, 2012; Marder, 2012; Bucher and Marder, 2013; Nadim and Bucher, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The pyloric circuit is sensitive to a plethora of small molecule transmitters and neuropeptides which affect cycle frequency and phase relationships.
source: The pyloric circuit is sensitive to a plethora of small molecule transmitters and neuropeptides which affect cycle frequency and phase relationships (Marder and Bucher, 2007; Stein, 2009; Daur et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Extensive research has indicated the role of amine modulation of synaptic strength and neuronal firing phase in the pyloric circuit.
source: Indeed, extensive research has indicated the role of amine modulation of synaptic strength and neuronal firing phase in the pyloric circuit, and how amine modulation of synaptic and intrinsic firing properties changes firing phases (Johnson et al., 2003; Gruhn et al., 2005; Johnson et al., 2005; Peck et al., 2006; Harris-Warrick and Johnson, 2010; Harris-Warrick, 2011; Kvarta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Any given neuromodulator could act presynaptically to alter P, duration, or duty cycle.
source: With respect to our findings, any given neuromodulator could act presynaptically to alter P, duration, or duty cycle on the one hand, and gmax and Δpeak on the other.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of neuromodulation.

claim: A neuromodulator could affect the postsynaptic neuron's properties and alter its sensitivity to synaptic parameters.
source: In addition, the neuromodulator could affect the postsynaptic neuron's properties and alter its sensitivity to any of these parameters.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of neuromodulation.

claim: The findings could provide a framework for testing if and how changes in synaptic dynamics may contribute to altering phase relationships under different neuromodulatory conditions.
source: Therefore, our findings could not just further our understanding of how phase can be maintained across different rhythm frequencies, but also provide a framework for testing if and how changes in synaptic dynamics may contribute to altering phase relationships under different neuromodulatory conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the findings.
